title: Singleness
hookLine: Paul and Jesus were single; celibacy is honored as a calling

cards: A wedding reception, table nine. The single friend gets the question again, from an aunt, kindly meant: so when's it your turn? Everyone laughs.
The friend laughs too, a half second late. Here's something that might surprise that aunt. The Gospels never mention a wife for Jesus.
And Paul tells the Corinthians he wishes more people could live as he does: unmarried. Two figures at the heart of the Christian story, and neither one is shown at a wedding of his own.

teach.h: EVERY MAN HATH HIS PROPER GIFT.
teach.b: Start with Paul's own words to the Corinthians: "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift.
Paul isn't saying single people are waiting for real life to begin, and he isn't saying married people have settled for less. Each way of life is a gift, and each person has their own.
He even gives a practical reason: the unmarried person can give undivided attention to the things of the Lord.
Jesus speaks of some who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and adds, he that is able to receive it, let him receive it. Not everyone, then. But some, as a calling.
Christians have honored that calling in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns make vows of celibacy.
In the Latin Catholic church, priests are ordinarily celibate; Orthodox priests may marry before they are ordained, though their bishops are chosen from the celibate.
Protestant churches don't require celibacy of their ministers, and they too honor single believers who serve with their whole lives.

And there's an older promise still, from Isaiah, to those who would never have children: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters."
A place and a name. Not someday, after a wedding. Already.
A single life, in this reading, isn't half of something.

how: Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns take vows of celibacy, and Latin-rite Catholic priests are ordinarily celibate; Christians across churches also honor single believers who serve in congregations, missions and communities.

o: a waiting time before your real life begins
a vow that only priests and nuns can take
a gift from God, as marriage is a gift

p: I would that all men were even as I

s: the Gospels mention a wife for Jesus

games.q: you're Paul, unmarried, writing to a church full of questions about marriage. what do you tell them about your own life?
o: that you wish more could live as you do, but each has their own gift.
that everyone must marry to serve God.
games.why: Paul wishes others could be "even as I myself," then adds that each has a proper gift from God, one this way, another that.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your life who is single, by choice, by circumstance, after loss, or simply not yet, and set aside every question about their dating life.

Look instead at what their life already holds, their work, the people they show up for, and name one thing clearly; if you're the single one, turn this toward yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Singleness. In Paul's words, a gift from God like marriage is a gift, and for some, a calling to serve with an undivided heart.

orig.note: Greek, 1 Corinthians 7:7: a gift, freely given.

carryVoice: Your line: whole already. A gift, in Paul's word, not a waiting room. See you tomorrow.
